Summary of the Gaps: Academia gave you deep research and writing habits, and the discipline to structure a complex argument, which helps when you organize a product's information. Research Analysis and Written Communication transfer. The bigger change here is the visual, hands-on craft: wireframing, prototyping, and shaping screens and flows, built on Interaction Design and Information Architecture. Your daily surface becomes Figma and FigJam rather than documents. The shift is from explaining ideas in words to showing them as things people can click, and from long solo work to fast, shared drafts.
Training Recommendations: Point your structured thinking at the making side. Start with Information Architecture, which rewards organizing complex material, then Interaction Design. Learn wireframing and prototyping in Figma on a real screen. Study a few strong design systems to see how the pieces fit. Learn Lean UX for the team rhythm. Lean on your writing to keep interfaces clear while the visual craft grows.
A Day in the Life: On a cross-functional team, your day is spent designing the screens and flows people use. You carry out and see through the making: wireframing layouts, building UI components and kits, developing information architecture, and turning ideas into clickable prototypes, with annotations that tell developers how it should behave. Beyond the screens you own, you are consulted across the team's work, weighing in on research, requirements, content, and product strategy, since design choices touch all of it. A typical day mixes focused design time in Figma and FigJam, sketching, wireframing, and refining a prototype, with collaboration: a standup, a critique where you show rough work for feedback, and a working session with researchers or engineers to keep the design grounded in real needs and buildable. You share drafts early and rough, and you refine in short loops rather than perfecting alone.
